sections.title: When's a good time to interrupt the user?
sections.subtitle: This is a case study I teach all my students. I start with real-world, relatable examples, then apply those principals to a storage upsell notification I worked on at Microsoft--with surprisingly counterintuitive results. The real lesson lies in elevating a one-off UX improvement to repeatable, systems-level impact.

callouts.text: If I drop my wallet, please, for the love of all that is good, interrupt whatever I'm doing to return it.
Sometimes an interruption prevents an even ruder interruption--in this case, running out of battery.
But not all interruptions are welcome. A bad notification interrupts the user without a clear reason to do so.

sections.heading: Here's where my students jump in
sections.content: With a shared definition of what constitutes a welcome vs unwelcome interruption (we don't call them notifications in my class!), we move on to my storage upsell example and see how we can improve upon it.

callouts.text: Buttons are vague and don't offer immediate solutions
Doesn't tie context to current storage needs
Notification triggers contextually when storage is almost full
Builds trust with an option for the user to manage their own storage needs

items.label: CRT lift
items.description: Anchored in-context prompt drove significantly higher direct action than the standard OS toast.

items.label: Conversion
items.description: Slightly fewer users purchased a new or upgraded storage plan

sections.heading: Why those results were a "failure", and how to fix them
sections.content:
Despite a massive 256% lift, due mostly to the option for users to manage storage themselves, we didn't extend this notification to everyone.

Why? Because the conversion rate didn't improve.

This part always shocks my class (I love a good plot twist), but it drives home how customer and business results come together. It's relatively easy to help students to learn how to design for just customers, or just business results.

But the real art of UX is finding solutions that help both users and the bottom line. So what would I have done differently? And, more importantly, what learnings should my students take from this example? There are three main lessons that lead to an entirely new set of key results...

callouts.text:
Lessons learned

  1. You are the customer's advocate. Losing a UX battle doesn't mean losing out on customer trust. Pushing for customer value, pointing out deceptive design patterns, and designing for a coherent user journey will bend your UX in a more human-centered direction.

  2. You're there to make the company money. The business comes first. So does the customer. Pleasing both is both the fun and challenging part of the job--relish it!

  3. Measure long-term trust, not just immediate results. And do it over time. Are CTRs steadily declining? Can you measure customer sentiment? In other words, how do the ~95% of users who don't click feel? Be patient, track it all, and make a broader argument that combines business results and customer needs.

items.label: Metric
items.description: Measuring CTR, conversion, and CSAT over time told a better story

items.label: Metric
items.description: Combined clear metrics and storytelling to get sign off from leadership

items.label: Metric
items.description: Durable patterns, backed by research, fed to an agentic language system

items.label: Metric
items.description: Time saved not building/ testing bad notifications can be measured in $

sections.heading: It's these concrete, tactical lessons that really juiced my impact, and helped my students
sections.content:
Teaching those lessons--not just the heuristics, metrics, and skills needed for good UX--is how my students are able to stand out in a tough job market.

At least two of my former students turned into coworkers at Microsoft. Dozens more now work at Amazon, TikTok, F5, and other Fortune 500 companies.
